provenance.projection: Genuine R4 claims retain every verdict, locator, rationale and supporting-source relationship. External source quote text is represented by its UTF-8 SHA256; exact original quotes and complete source bodies are retained and supplied to the independent data reviewer. This is a labeled projection, not an object-identical full native review. Private native reasoning is excluded. Read-coverage quotations are omitted; original 87-input declaration is retained privately. No new source judgment is asserted.
provenance.review_budget: Whole-page and content-PR streams each stop at valid unchanged R4 approval, 4 of 5 spent. This data PR is a separate scoped transfer review and does not reset either stream.

findings.quote: Any time a computer is slow, full, hot, or unreliable
findings.why: Question, not a restored mechanism. The deleted sentence 'A hot laptop can slow its CPU to protect itself' is absent. This cell lists complaints for which the learner should name a resource. 'Hot' is not paired with the sourced turbo limit (boost only to the heat the system can tolerate) and does not say heat throttles the CPU. A novice could still treat heat as a fifth resource the page no longer checks.
findings.fix: Drop 'hot' from that cell, or add one sourced clause that higher clocks and turbo depend on tolerable heat, without saying a hot laptop slows its CPU to protect itself.

finding_disposition.R4-F1: Deferred optional low-confidence nit; exact approved page/seed unchanged. Never treated as support for a thermal mechanism.

claims.rationale: The control-plane and Windows-worker split matches, and the laptop OS is kept separate. No server-prevalence claim remains. The later-exercises clause is this curriculum's route, not a market share.

supporting_sources.rationale: Authored curriculum-route clause only. Sibling lessons were not audited.

claims.rationale: The lesson reports Whirlwind in 1953 and one bit per ring, and separates that from modern volatile RAM. It does not repeat the page's first-use claim.

supporting_sources.rationale: One bit per core.

claims.rationale: They taped it into the log. 'In the machine' is broader than 'in one of the components' and is not a contradiction. The lesson says the moth did not originate the term.

supporting_sources.rationale: The term predates 1947.

claims.locator: Resource Management for Pods and Containers
claims.rationale: Processor, working memory, durable storage, and OS coordination match the sourced CPU, RAM, storage, and OS pages. Larger systems still have those limits.

supporting_sources.rationale: Active memory needs power.

claims.rationale: Container memory limits are in P01S12. Disk pressure is this page. The next-module clause is navigation.

supporting_sources.rationale: Container memory limits.

claims.rationale: OS coordination of memory and files is supported here and by file access checks. The manager wording is the labeled analogy.

supporting_sources.rationale: The OS allows or denies file access.

claims.rationale: The processor executes the work. 'Heat' in the same sentence is a recipe verb in the labeled analogy, not a thermal-throttling claim.
The lesson limits volatility to the modern laptop and server examples and points ahead to a different historical implementation.
SSD and HDD are the named mechanisms. The lesson says durability still needs backups and does not claim devices cannot fail.

supporting_sources.rationale: HDD side of the contrast.

claims.rationale: A terminal hosts that interpreter. 'Decoding data' here is a browser-recipe description, not a video-call codec or CPU-saturation claim.

supporting_sources.locator: What is the difference between a shell and a terminal?
supporting_sources.rationale: Terminal versus shell.

claims.rationale: Too little resident working memory forces extra movement. Adding storage does not replace that workspace. The kitchen wording is the analogy under the stated premise.

supporting_sources.locator: View memory usage in Activity Monitor
supporting_sources.rationale: Pressure is a memory condition, not free disk space.

claims.rationale: The processor executes machine instructions. The lesson states that the analogy is not the internal implementation.
CPU, RAM, storage, and OS or program behavior are alternative bottlenecks, each hedged with 'may'. The paragraph does not state a law.
Instruction execution is CPU work. Whether another processor is faster depends on workload and design, which is what the lesson says.
Parallel use depends on the software. Hyper-Threading is only on some CPUs. The brand names are examples of labels, not a roster to memorize.

supporting_sources.rationale: Not every core exposes two hardware threads.

claims.rationale: Gigahertz means billions of cycles. The same article says a higher clock is not the whole comparison, and turbo is limited by heat and cores in use. Cooling and power limits name that heat budget. The page does not say a hot laptop slows the CPU to protect itself.

supporting_sources.rationale: Gigahertz as billions of cycles.
Heat and core use bound the clock. This is not the deleted protection-slowdown sentence.

claims.rationale: Pageable code and data are brought in on reference, so opening a program does not require every page to be resident. Volatility is the Kingston entry.

supporting_sources.rationale: Unsaved RAM contents are at risk if power disappears. 'At risk' is the right strength.

claims.rationale: Apple also documents reclaimable cache and Swap Used. A hard fault reads a paging file or mapped file. Linux top documents an OOM score used when memory is exhausted, which supports 'in severe cases' rather than a universal kill.

supporting_sources.rationale: Moving pages to backing store.
Severe exhaustion can end a task on Linux. Not every OS.

claims.rationale: Tab count is not a measured bottleneck. The answer requires pressure and swap checks. The removed 4–6 GB claim is not in this sentence.

A slow video edit can justify checking CPU, and editing may use several cores. The lesson also requires memory and storage checks and says a symptom alone does not establish the cause. It does not assert saturation, encoding, decoding, or a purchase.

supporting_sources.rationale: The required memory check.

claims.rationale: hw.memsize is RAM size in bytes. The retained stdout is 17179869184, equal to 16×2^30, and About on that Mac recorded 16GB. The brand_string command's retained stdout is 'Apple M4'. The Apple JSON does not define that key, and the 404 page is not used. df -h / on that Mac printed filesystem usage for /. The sentence does not claim every Mac prints these values.

supporting_sources.rationale: Human-readable processor description on that host.
Readable filesystem usage including the root mount.

claims.rationale: The current sentence no longer says the commands are common on servers. free -h and df -h match their manuals. The container stdout shows lscpu emitted a processor summary in that guest only.

supporting_sources.rationale: free summarizes memory.
df -h is human-readable filesystem space.

claims.rationale: The figures can differ. 'Firmware reservations' names that BIOS example, not a second mechanism. Settings > System > About lists installed RAM. This is documentation support. Windows execution was not done.

supporting_sources.rationale: Name is the processor label.
About is the installed-RAM inventory.
FileSystem drives expose used and free space.

claims.rationale: A description or one percentage does not establish a bottleneck. The lesson requires activity and pressure before a change.
RAM contrasts with storage that keeps files across power-off. Saving is the copy from working memory to storage. A successful write is not automatically durable.

supporting_sources.rationale: Saved is not automatically durable.

claims.rationale: HDD means spinning platters and moving parts. SSD means NAND without a moving arm.

supporting_sources.rationale: SSD definition.

claims.rationale: Moving parts add seek time. This is a vendor comparison, and the lesson does not universalize it.
No mechanical seek. The lesson does not say every SSD is faster for every workload.

claims.locator: Examples and comparisons with SI prefixes
claims.rationale: The same capture gives 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes = 1,073,741,824 bytes, so a GiB is larger than that GB. Decimal tera over giga is 10^3, so one decimal terabyte is 1,000 GB. The direct NIST HTTP body is ineligible.

supporting_sources.rationale: GiB figure used by the lesson.

claims.rationale: Unsaved RAM is at risk. Previously saved data can still be hurt by a short or interrupted write. 'Normally' matches that limit.

supporting_sources.rationale: An interrupted write can leave a partial update.

claims.rationale: A full filesystem can block writes while CPU and RAM remain available. Swap also uses disk space. 'May' keeps the strength right.

supporting_sources.rationale: Swap needs disk space.
